newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-New Thai indicators seen as mildly positive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New Thai indicators seen as mildly positive.

text.p: Thai economic indicators for December and January released by the finance ministry on Wednesday showed a mild positive trend but failed to show that a national economic slowdown had bottomed out, analysts said.
The indicators showed that the December trade and current account deficits narrowed to 22.3 billion and 19.1 billion baht from 24.2 billion and 21.7 billion respectively in November.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said the smaller December deficits helped curb the current account deficit for the whole 1996 to 8.0 percent of gross domestic product against 8.2 percent estimated earlier by the central bank and an actual 8.1 percent in 1995.

But analysts said although latest monthly figures on industrial output and private investment showed some recovery, there were no indications that economic sluggishness seen since the second half of 1996 had been reversed.

"All growth indicators still look pretty anaemic. The question now is not whether we can bring inflation and current account deficit under control. What we should ask is whether most companies can survive the current downturn without going bankrupt first," an analyst at a Thai finance firm said.

The ministry figures said the December manufacturing index posted 4.8 percent year-on-year growth which, although higher than 4.1 percent in November, was still far below average expansion of over 10 percent that Thailand experienced during the first half of the 1990s.
The December private investment index eased further to 7.5 percent year-on-year growth from 7.8 percent in November and 14.3 percent a year ago.

The ministry said total outstanding loans extended by Thai commercial banks continued its downward growth trend, rising about 13.7 percent year-on-year in January against 14.3 percent in December and 22.9 percent a year ago.

Another analyst at Dhana Siam Finance and Securities said it was premature to say whether the latest improving indicators could be sustained at a pace to have an impact on a current review downwards of Thailand's long-term sovereign debts by Moody's Investors Service.

She said although the monthly current account deficit had been on a clear and steady declining trend in the past few months, foreign analysts had turned to focus on vulnerable financial positions of some financial institutions especially those with big loan exposures to the property sector.

The analyst said her foreign colleagues also watched the private sector's short-term foreign loans which were responsible for raising the country's total foreign debts to about $89.6 billion at end-December.
The ministry figures, however, said that short-term debts accounted for 43.7 percent of total foreign borrowing in December against 49.8 percent a year earlier.
